# Volume 2 — XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

A certain day in May brought a slight flutter of excitement to the people of Brierley on account of some “Brierley Notes” bearing the signature “Observer,” which were published in the Port Marlow Daily Enterprise. Local rumors credited Wilfred Mott with writing them, owing in part to the fact that the aforementioned Wilfred had penned comparable pieces of writing in the past, and owing in part to the appearance of a mockery directed at Hugh Carrow in one of the items. The youth of Brierley continued to view Hugh Carrow and Wilfred Mott as competitors seeking the favor of a particular young lady who possessed gray eyes and an imaginative mind.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0000 }

Rumors, as was typically the case, were incorrect. The messages were authored by Hugh Carrow, who was helped and encouraged by Nell, and he included the message regarding himself to mislead everyone. Merely two among the notes possess any relevance to this account:
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0001 }

“Word is going around that a marriage is set to take place in our village before the daisies bloom. An inhabitant who is both new and greatly esteemed will escort one of our most well-liked women to the nuptial altar.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0002 }

“Our famous forecaster of the weather, Uncle Zeb, forecasts that a severe tempest with lightning and thunder will occur on the night of May twenty-third, commencing precisely at seven o’clock. Most of the Province will be included in the region affected by the storm. Individuals who are journeying during that evening would be wise to bring along mackintoshes and umbrellas.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0003 }

“A storm for some point this spring has indeed been foretold by Uncle Zeb,” Hugh remarked, “yet do you believe that Isabella Pullen is truly visited by Mr. Pettifer?”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0004 }

“No,” Nell said with a laugh, “I am certain his sole purpose is playing checkers alongside Mr. Pettifer Pullen, yet according to Mrs. Sowerby, she is positive Isabella Pullen is bound to wed soon, given how cheerful she has been throughout this spring.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0005 }

The notes made poor old Uncle Zeb feel somewhat indignant. That “Observer” was mocking him was his suspicion. Although he furiously repudiated having set a specific date for his storm, he was believed by nobody.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0006 }

Existence in Brierley proceeded along its calm and uniform course. The "planting" was accomplished; an Arbor Day was observed by the Improvers. Every single Improver planted, or arranged to have planted, five decorative trees. Because the organization currently comprised forty members, a grand total of two hundred saplings resulted from this. The red fields turned green with early oats; great blossoming branches were wrapped around the farmhouses by apple orchards, and the Frost Maiden beautified itself like a bride preparing for her groom. Nell preferred sleeping with an open window so that the aroma of cherries could drift across her face throughout the night. It struck her as extremely poetical. Thirza believed her life was being put at risk.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0007 }

“Thanksgiving ought to be kept in the springtime,” Nell remarked to Thirza one night, while the two of them were sitting on the front door steps and listening to the frogs’ silver-sweet chorus. “It seems to me it would be so much preferable to holding it in November, when all things are deceased or dormant. At that time you are forced to recollect to be thankful; whereas in May a person just cannot prevent being thankful . . . because they are living, if for no other reason. My feelings are precisely what Eve’s must have been in the garden of Eden prior to the trouble starting. Does that grass in the hollow look green or golden? Thirza, it strikes me that a gem of a day such as this, with the blossoms open and the winds unsure which direction to blow from next out of pure wild joy, must be almost as wonderful as heaven.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0008 }

Thirza appeared shocked and cast an anxious look about her to ensure that the twins were out of hearing range. At that precise moment, they rounded the corner of the dwelling.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0009 }

“Ain’t it an awful nice-smelling evening?” Robin inquired, inhaling with joy while wielding a hoe with dirty hands. He had been laboring in his plot. During that spring, Thirza, hoping to direct Robin’s love of playing with clay and mud toward productive ends, had provided a tiny patch of land to him and Lucy to serve as a garden. Each child had enthusiastically begun working in a distinct manner. Lucy executed her planting, weeding, and watering with care, system, and a lack of emotion. Consequently, neat, organized small lines of annuals and vegetables made her plot green already. On the other hand, Robin labored with greater enthusiasm than judgment; his digging, hoeing, raking, watering, and transplanting were done so vigorously that the seeds he planted were denied any opportunity to survive.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0010 }

“In what manner is your plot of land progressing, Robin-boy?” inquired Nell.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0011 }

“Rather sluggish,” Robin uttered, sighing. “The reason these things fail to thrive more escapes me. Milty Gammon claims the entire problem stems from me planting them during the moon's dark phase. According to him, sowing seeds, slaughtering pigs, trimming hair, or performing any crucial task during an incorrect lunar phase is something you must never do. Does truth lie in that, Nell? Knowledge of this is what I seek.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0012 }

“Perhaps if you refrained from yanking your plants out by their roots every couple of days just to check their progress ‘at the other end,’ they might thrive,” Thirza remarked sarcastically.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0013 }

“I merely yanked up six of them,” Robin objected. “I wished to check for grubs at the roots. Milty Gammon stated that if the fault did not lie with the moon, grubs were responsible. However, I discovered merely a single grub. It was a huge, moist, bent grub. Placing him on a rock, I retrieved a second rock and crushed him completely. I am telling you, he produced a splendid sqush. I felt regretful that they were not more numerous. The planting of Lucy’s garden occurred at the same time as mine, yet her plants are developing properly. The moon cannot be to blame,” Robin decided thoughtfully.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0014 }

“Thirza, glance over at that apple tree,” Nell remarked. “Why, it resembles a person. Extending its lengthy arms, it delicately gathers its own pink skirts to entice our praise.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0015 }

“Those Yellow Duchess trees never fail to yield a good crop,” Thirza remarked with satisfaction. “There will be a heavy load on that tree this year. I am truly pleased. . . they make excellent pies.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0016 }

Yet neither Thirza nor Nell nor anyone at all was destined to bake pies from Yellow Duchess apples during that year.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0017 }

May twenty-third arrived . . . it was a day that was abnormally hot, a fact no one understood more sharply than Nell together with her tiny cluster of students, who were sweating through syntax and fractions inside the schoolroom at Brierley. Throughout the entire morning, a warm wind gusted; however, following the lunch hour, it vanished into a thick quietness. Nell caught the faint sound of rolling thunder at three-thirty. She immediately let the pupils out of school right then, in order for the youngsters to reach home prior to the arrival of the tempest.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0018 }

While they walked out toward the playground, Nell noticed that a particular darkness and somberness hung over the world, even though the sun continued to shine brilliantly. Annetta Bell anxiously grabbed her hand.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0019 }

“Oh, instructor, observe that terrible cloud!”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0020 }

Nell stared and uttered a cry of distress. A collection of clouds, unlike any she had ever seen in her entire existence, was swiftly rising in the northwest. It was completely black, except where its twisted and feathered margins displayed an eerie, deathly white. As it loomed in the unclouded blue sky, there was an indefinable threat to it; every so often a flash of lightning darted across it, which was succeeded by a fierce rumble. Descending so close to the earth, it appeared nearly to brush the summits of the forest-covered hills.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0021 }

Mr. Gorham Pullen arrived noisily up the slope aboard his truck wagon, driving his pair of grays as fast as they could go. Right across from the school, he brought the horses to a stop.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0022 }

“Nell, it looks like Uncle Zeb was actually right this single time,” he yelled out. “That storm of his is arriving a small bit early. Have you ever set eyes on a cloud like that one? Come on, every one of you kids who is traveling in my direction, hop inside, while those of you who aren’t must run quickly to the post office should you have farther than a quarter of a mile left to walk, and remain in that place until the rain passes.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0023 }

Grabbing Robin and Lucy by their hands, Nell raced down the incline, traversed the Aspen Path, and hurried past Primrose Dell and Reedmere at the maximum speed the twins' chubby legs could manage. Arriving at Grey Shutters just in time, they met Thirza at the entrance, who had been hurriedly driving her chickens and ducks to cover. The moment they burst into the kitchen, the light appeared to disappear, like a giant breath had extinguished it; the terrifying cloud swept across the sun, casting a darkness akin to late twilight over the land. Simultaneously, accompanied by a thunderous crash and an intense flash of lightning, the hail descended fiercely, erasing the surrounding scenery in a single blanket of white rage.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0024 }

Amidst the whole din of the tempest arrived the impact of severed boughs hitting the home alongside the harsh snapping of shattering glass. Within three minutes all the panes within the western and northern windows were shattered and the hail streamed inside via the gaps burying the floor in stones, with the tiniest among them being equal in size to an egg of a hen. For forty-five minutes the tempest stormed without lessening and not a single person who endured it ever erased it from memory. Thirza, driven out of her calmness for a single time in her existence by pure fright, was kneeling beside her rocking chair within a kitchen corner, panting and weeping in the intervals of the blaring thunder claps. Nell, pale like paper, had pulled the couch from the window and was sitting upon it flanked by a twin on each side. Robin during the initial impact had cried, “Nell, Nell, is it the Judgment Day? Nell, Nell, I never meant to be naughty,” before burying his face against Nell’s lap and maintaining it in place, his small frame shaking. Lucy, rather pale yet entirely calm, was sitting while holding hands with Nell, silent and still. It remains questionable whether an earthquake could have unsettled Lucy.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0025 }

Then, nearly as abruptly as it had started, the tempest died down. The hail ceased, the thunder rumbled and growled off toward the east, and the sun broke through bright and cheerful upon an earth so altered that believing a mere forty-five minutes could have wrought such a change felt ridiculous.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0026 }

Rising from her knees in a feeble and shaking state, Thirza collapsed onto her rocking chair. She possessed a drawn face and appeared a decade older.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0027 }

“Is everyone out of there with their lives?” she inquired gravely.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0028 }

“We certainly have,” Robin chimed in bright spirits, having fully recovered himself. “And I wasn’t frightened in the least . . . except right at the start. It struck a guy so abruptly. In the blink of an eye, I decided against fighting Teddy Mott Monday like I’d agreed to; but perhaps I’ll do it after all now. Tell me, Lucy, did you feel afraid?”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0029 }

“Indeed, I felt somewhat frightened,” Lucy remarked in a proper manner, “yet I gripped Nell’s hand firmly and continuously recited my prayers.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0030 }

“Indeed, I would have uttered my prayers as well had it crossed my mind,” Robin stated; “however,” he appended with a victorious air, “you can see that I survived precisely as unharmed as you despite not having uttered them.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0031 }

Nell fetched a glass of her strong currant wine for Thirza . . . Nell had known all too well, during her younger years, just how strong it was . . . and after that, the two of them walked over to the doorway so they could gaze out at the unusual sight.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0032 }

A knee-deep, white carpet of hailstones stretched far and wide; beneath the eaves and upon the steps, drifts of them had piled high. Those hailstones thawed three or four days afterward, whereupon the devastation they had caused became clearly visible, because all green plants growing within the garden or field were severed. The apple trees lost not only every single blossom, but also huge branches and boughs that were ripped off. Furthermore, out of the two hundred trees planted by the Improvers, the vast majority were shredded or broken in two.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0033 }

“Is there any way this is still the identical world from an hour before?” Nell inquired, in a daze. “Playing this much havoc must have required more time.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0034 }

“Nothing like this has ever occurred on St. Brendan’s Island,” Thirza remarked, “ever. A severe storm took place when I was a young girl, as I recall, though it could not compare to this one. You can be certain that we will learn of dreadful ruin.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0035 }

“I do hope none of the children were caught out in it,” Nell anxiously murmured. As was found out afterwards, not a single child had been, because every one who had some way to travel had followed Mr. Pullen’ excellent advice and taken shelter in the post office.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0036 }

“John Henry Carter is arriving,” Thirza stated.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0037 }

John Henry approached, striding through the hail with an expression that was frightened yet smiling.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0038 }

“Oh, isn’t this terrible, Miss Abernethy? I was sent over by Mr. Pettifer to check whether yous had emerged unscathed.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0039 }

“Not one of us has been killed,” Thirza stated with a grim expression, “and not a single building was hit. It is my hope that you fared just as well.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0040 }

“Yas’m. A bit worse, ma’am. Our place got hit. The lightning brought down the kitchen chimbly, traveled through the flue, overturned Nutmeg’s cage, ripped a hole through the floor, and entered the sullar. Yas’m.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0041 }

“Did Nutmeg sustain any injuries?” Nell asked.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0042 }

“Yas’m. He was hurt pretty bad. He was killed.” Afterward, Nell crossed over to offer comfort to Mr. Pettifer. She discovered him seated beside the table, a shaking hand caressing the bright, lifeless form of Nutmeg.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0043 }

“Nutmeg won’t be calling you names again, Nell, poor thing,” he uttered sorrowfully.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0044 }

It had never occurred to Nell that Nutmeg could make her weep, yet tears welled up in her eyes.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0045 }

“Nell, he was the only companion I possessed . . . and now he has passed away. Oh well, caring this deeply just proves I am a foolish old man. I will pretend that it doesn't bother me. I am aware you intend to offer words of comfort the moment I grow quiet . . . but please refrain. Should you say anything, I would weep like an infant. Wasn't the tempest dreadful? It seems unlikely that people will mock the forecasts of Uncle Zeb in the future. It appears that every single storm he foretold throughout his existence that failed to materialize arrived simultaneously. Isn't it extraordinary how he hit upon the precise date, nevertheless? Observe the disaster surrounding us. I need to hurry about and locate a few planks to repair the opening in the flooring.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0046 }

The following day was spent by Brierley folks solely in visiting one another to assess their losses. Because hailstones made the roads impossible for wheeled vehicles, travel was done on foot or on horses. Disastrous news from every corner of the province arrived with the delayed mail. Lightning had struck houses, leaving people dead and hurt; total disruption had hit the telephone and telegraph networks, while countless young farm animals left out in the pastures had died.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0047 }

Early in the morning, Uncle Zeb waded out to the blacksmith’s forge, where he remained for the entire day. This was Uncle Zeb’s moment of victory, and he took complete pleasure in it. Saying Uncle Zeb felt happy about the storm's occurrence would be an injustice to him; however, given that it was destined to occur, he felt immense joy at having forecasted it . . . precisely to the day, as well. Uncle Zeb lost all recollection of ever having disclaimed fixing the date. Regarding the minor difference in the time, it was of no consequence.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0048 }

It was evening when Hugh reached Grey Shutters, where he discovered Thirza and Nell hard at work as they nailed pieces of oilcloth to cover the shattered windowpanes.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0049 }

“Heaven alone can tell the time we will receive glass to fit them,” stated Thirza. “Although Mr. Pembroke travelled across to Delford earlier today, he was unable to secure even one pane regardless of what he offered. By ten o’clock, the residents of Delford had completely emptied Lawson and Blair. Did you experience a severe storm over at Pale Sands, Hugh?”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0050 }

“I certainly would. Having been trapped inside the school alongside every child, I believed a few might be driven insane by terror. Three children lost consciousness, while a pair of girls suffered hysterical fits, and Tommy Scobie endlessly screamed as loudly as he could throughout the entire ordeal.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0051 }

“A single squeal was all I uttered,” Robin declared with pride. “Everything in my garden had been flattened,” he went on sadly, “though Lucy’s suffered the exact same fate,” he remarked with an attitude showing that Gilead still possessed its balm.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0052 }

Sprinting down from the west gable, Nell approached.
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0053 }

“Oh, Hugh, have you received word? The former residence of Mr. Levi Gammon was hit and completely consumed by fire. I feel as though I am terribly sinful for being pleased about it, considering how much harm occurred. According to Mr. Gammon, he thinks the B.V.I.S. conjured that tempest intentionally.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0054 }

“Indeed, a single fact cannot be denied,” Hugh uttered with a laugh, “‘Observer’ has established the renown of Uncle Zeb as a forecaster of conditions. In the annals of this area, ‘Uncle Zeb’s storm’ shall be remembered. That its arrival coincided precisely with the date chosen by us is a truly remarkable event. A sense of slight culpability genuinely affects me, as though the tempest was summoned by my own sorcery. Since the destruction of our young trees leaves little cause for celebration, we might as well take pleasure in the destruction of the former residence. Under ten of those saplings remain standing.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0055 }

“Oh, indeed, we are simply required to sow them once more when the coming spring arrives,” Nell observed with resignation. “Such is a single positive aspect regarding our existence . . . we can perpetually count on further springs to come.”
{: #nw-v02-c24-p0056 }
